title: Amar Das and Ram Das
hook: then Guru Amar Das and Guru Ram Das, who are our help

segments.voice: Yesterday: Angad, and your line: nanak, angad, the first handover. Today the same line of the Ardas names the third and fourth Gurus.

Most people, at seventy-three, are slowing down. Sikh tradition tells of a man who, at that age, was still carrying water before dawn, every day, for his teacher. One stormy night, the story goes, he stumbled and fell into a weaver's pit, and the weaver's wife laughed at the homeless old man. Not long after, that old man became the third Guru. And the young man he would later choose was another servant, an orphan who had sold boiled grain on the street as a boy. Two people the world overlooked. The Ardas names them together, and asks them for something.
screen: `SEVENTY-THREE, AND STILL CARRYING WATER.` → `A STREET SELLER, ORPHANED.` → `TWO PEOPLE THE WORLD OVERLOOKED.`

segments.voice: The Ardas line runs on from Angad: amar daas, raam daasai, hoeen sahai. Amar Das and Ram Das: be our help. Notice that verb. The Ardas doesn't just remember these two; it asks them to stand by us. Sahai, the helper, is a word we met in the saloks: You alone are the helper. Guru Amar Das became Guru in 1552, already in his seventies, after years of serving Guru Angad. He's remembered for making the langar a rule: pehle pangat, phir sangat, first sit in the line and eat, then join the gathering. Rich or poor, high caste or low, everyone sat on the same floor. Tradition says even the emperor Akbar sat in that line before meeting him. He organized the growing community into regions with appointed leaders, built a stepped well at Goindwal, and spoke against practices that harmed women, including sati. Guru Ram Das, born Jetha, was the orphan who sold grain. He came to Goindwal, served in the kitchen, married the Guru's daughter, Bibi Bhani, and became the fourth Guru in 1574. He founded the town that grew into Amritsar and began the pool at its heart. And he wrote the Lavan, the four verses of every Sikh wedding, sung as the couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib. So these two names carry a kitchen floor where everyone is equal, a city and a wedding hymn. Both men began as servants. That's the pattern the Ardas keeps reminding Sikhs of: the ones who served became the ones who help.
screen: `AMAR DAS, RAM DAS: BE OUR HELP.` · `PEHLE PANGAT: FIRST, THE SHARED FLOOR.` · `RAM DAS: A CITY AND THE LAVAN.` · `THE SERVANTS BECAME THE HELP.` · then, large: `AMAR DAS, RAM DAS.`

segments.voice: Let the names ride on the in-breath: Amar Das, and an old man with a water pot in the dark; then Ram Das, and a young man stirring a pot in a crowded kitchen, with each out-breath long and empty between them. If you pray, add the Ardas's own words, hoeen sahai, be our help. If you don't, think of someone whose quiet service you've overlooked.
Amar Das. The third Guru, a servant first; the Ardas asks him, hoeen sahai, be our help.
Your line: amar das, ram das. Two servants, and now the Ardas asks them for help. Day six hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember Guru Amar Das and Guru Ram Das and ask them to be their help; Guru Amar Das's langar rule and Guru Ram Das's Lavan are still part of Sikh life.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Ardas only lists Amar Das and Ram Das.
what it means: it asks them for help: hoeen sahai, be our help.
what a scholar hears: Guru Amar Das organized the manji system and the Goindwal baoli; Guru Ram Das's Lavan in Raag Suhi (Ang 773) became the core of the Anand Karaj.

chat.says: Why does everyone sit on the floor together at langar?
options: Guru Amar Das made it a rule: first eat side by side, rich or poor, then gather.
Because the early gurdwaras were too poor to afford tables and chairs.
It's a lesson in humility that only newcomers are asked to accept.
chat.meaning: Pehle pangat, phir sangat: first sit in the line and eat, then join the gathering. Everyone shares the same floor.
